nuance.etymology: A modern American colloquialism; plain words ("this is what I meant") turned into a cheer, heard especially in sports.
common_mistakes: Using a flat tone; it needs excitement.
Saying "that's what I talk about"; it is progressive: "I'm talking."

word: tell me something I don't know

senses: Said when someone tells you something obvious or something you already know well (often wearily).

etymology: Plain words used as an ironic reply: the speaker pretends to ask for news because what was said is old news.

conversation.text: "Traffic's bad on Fridays." "Tell me something I don't know."
"Your brother can be really stubborn." "Tell me something I don't know."

core.definition: I already know that very well.

pronunciation.respelling: tel mee suhm-thing ahy dohnt NOH
pronunciation.tip: Stress KNOW, with DON'T also strong: tel-mee-SUHM-thing-ahy-DOHNT-NOH.

nuance.connotation: Wry, weary or slightly impatient.
nuance.usage_note: A reply to a statement of the obvious, often a complaint you share. Said dryly, it is friendly; said sharply, it can sound rude. Often heard about a person you both know.

distinctions.note: "Tell me about it" agrees with a complaint from experience; "tell me something I don't know" says the comment is obvious.
"No kidding" can express surprise or, sarcastically, that something is obvious.
"You're telling me" means I know that better than you do.

collocations: Tell me something I don't know.
Ha, tell me something I don't know.

examples.everyday: "Teenagers sleep a lot." "Tell me something I don't know. Mine got up at two today."
examples.professional: "The legacy system is slow." "Tell me something I don't know."
examples.analytical: "Tell me something I don't know" signals that information is redundant, a quick way to mark shared knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Like being handed a map of your own neighborhood.
nuance.etymology: Plain words used as an ironic reply: the speaker pretends to ask for news because what was said is old news.
common_mistakes: Taking it as a sincere request for new information.
Saying "tell me something I didn't know"; the usual form is "don't know."

senses: Go slowly and carefully (said when someone is moving, lifting or handling something).
Calm down; don't get too excited or angry.

etymology: A colloquial saying meaning that a gentle approach gets the job done; origin uncertain.

conversation.text: Easy does it. Lift with your legs, not your back.
Easy does it, guys. It's just a board game.

core.definition: Slowly and carefully; take it easy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress DOES. "Does it" blends: DUH-zit.

nuance.connotation: Calm, gentle and caring.
nuance.usage_note: Often said while helping: carrying furniture, backing up a car, helping someone stand up. In the second sense it calms someone down. Also a slogan in recovery groups, meaning don't rush.

distinctions.note: "Take it easy" means relax or goodbye; "easy does it" means slow down and be careful in what you're doing right now.
"Go easy on someone" means don't be too harsh with them.
"Hold your horses" means wait, don't rush ahead.

collocations: Easy does it on the stairs.

examples.everyday: Easy does it with that box; it's full of dishes.
examples.professional: Easy does it on the rollout; let's start with one region before going national.
examples.analytical: "Easy does it" captures the principle that slow, controlled actions reduce errors and accidents.

nuance.analogy: Like lowering a sleeping baby into a crib.
nuance.etymology: A colloquial saying meaning that a gentle approach gets the job done; origin uncertain.
common_mistakes: Saying "easy do it"; it is "does."
Using it to mean "it's easy"; it means "be careful."

senses: It's not surprising; that explains it (said when you learn the reason for something).

etymology: From "wonder" in the sense of surprise or amazement: there is no cause for surprise.

conversation.text: "I didn't sleep last night." "No wonder you're so tired."
Oh, the oven was off the whole time? No wonder the cake didn't rise.

core.definition: That explains it; of course.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WON. "Wonder" sounds like WUHN-der, not like "wander."

nuance.connotation: Neutral; can be sympathetic or a little teasing.
nuance.usage_note: Used as a reply ("No wonder!") or at the start of a sentence ("No wonder he's upset"). It reacts to a newly learned cause. "It's no wonder (that)..." and "Small wonder..." are a bit more formal.

distinctions.note: "That figures" means "that is what I expected," often about something disappointing; "no wonder" means "now I understand why."
"Go figure" means "strange, I can't explain it," the opposite of "no wonder."
"Small wonder" means the same and sounds more formal or written.

examples.everyday: "The battery was in backward." "No wonder the remote wasn't working."
examples.professional: It's no wonder the team is burned out after three months of weekend work.
examples.analytical: "No wonder" marks the moment an observed effect is linked to its cause.

nuance.analogy: Like finding the light switch was off after wondering why the lamp was broken.
nuance.etymology: From "wonder" in the sense of surprise or amazement: there is no cause for surprise.
common_mistakes: Writing "no wander"; "wander" means to walk around.
Saying "no wonder" before the cause; it follows hearing the cause: "Oh, it was unplugged? No wonder."

senses: Said when a topic annoys you so much that you could complain about it for a long time (often followed by a complaint anyway).

etymology: From "get someone started" (on a subject), to set them talking about a favorite complaint.

conversation.text: "How's your new landlord?" "Ugh, don't get me started."
Airline fees? Don't get me started. Last week they charged me forty bucks for a carry-on.

core.definition: That topic really bothers me, and I could go on about it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress START. The t in "started" is often a flap: STAHR-did.

nuance.connotation: Exasperated, usually humorous.
nuance.usage_note: A warning that a topic is a sore point. Often ironic, because the speaker starts complaining right after. "Don't even get me started" is a more emphatic variant. It is a natural way to show strong feelings without a long rant.

distinctions.note: "Tell me about it" agrees with someone else's complaint; "don't get me started" announces your own.
"Don't go there" asks someone not to raise a topic; "don't get me started" says the topic annoys you.

examples.everyday: "Have you tried parking downtown lately?" "Don't get me started."
examples.professional: "How's the new expense system?" "Don't get me started; it took me an hour to file one receipt."
examples.analytical: "Don't get me started" both signals a strong grievance and invites the listener to ask for more.

nuance.analogy: Like a soda bottle that's been shaken: open it and it all comes out.
nuance.etymology: From "get someone started" (on a subject), to set them talking about a favorite complaint.
common_mistakes: Saying "don't make me start"; the idiom is "don't get me started."
Using it about something you like; it is about things that annoy you.
